claim: Growth rate correlates strongly with fitness in microbes.
source: For microbes, growth rate correlates strongly with fitness (Orr, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Orr, 2009

claim: Cells increase growth rates through balancing their synthesis of ribosomes with their intake of nutrients.
source: Cells increase growth rates through balancing their synthesis of ribosomes with their intake of nutrients (Broach, 2012; Levy and Barkai, 2009; Scott et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Broach, 2012; Levy and Barkai, 2009; Scott et al., 2014

claim: Cells target a particular size through coordinating growth with division.
source: target a particular size through coordinating growth with division (Johnston et al., 1977; Jorgensen et al., 2004; Di Talia et al., 2007; Turner et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Johnston et al., 1977; Jorgensen et al., 2004; Di Talia et al., 2007; Turner et al., 2012

claim: Time-lapse microscopy with microfluidic technology has been pivotal for studying single cells.
source: Time-lapse microscopy, particularly with microfluidic technology to control the extracellular environment (Locke and Elowitz, 2009; Bennett and Hasty, 2009), has been pivotal
evidence: Supported by citations to Locke and Elowitz, 2009; Bennett and Hasty, 2009

claim: S. cerevisiae grows by forming a bud that increases in size while the volume of the rest of the cell remains relatively unchanged.
source: S. cerevisiae grows by forming a bud that increases in size while the volume of the rest of the cell remains relatively unchanged.
evidence: Statement about the biological process of budding yeast growth

claim: Single-cell growth rate is typically reported as the rate of change of volume.
source: Although single-cell growth rate is typically reported as the rate of change of volume (Ferrezuelo et al., 2012; Soifer et al., 2016; Chandler-Brown et al., 2017; Leitao and Kellogg, 2017; Garmendia-Torres et al., 2018; Litsios et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Growth rates for budding yeast are often only reported for isolated cells using low-throughput and semi-automated methods.
source: Growth rates for budding yeast are therefore often only reported for isolated cells using low-throughput and semi-automated methods (Ferrezuelo et al., 2012; Litsios et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ferrezuelo et al., 2012; Litsios et al., 2019

claim: For rod-shaped cells that divide symmetrically, like Escherichia coli, the growth rate can be found more simply, as the rate of change of a cell's length.
source: In contrast, for rod-shaped cells that divide symmetrically, like Escherichia coli, the growth rate can be found more simply, as the rate of change of a cell's length (Kiviet et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kiviet et al., 2014

claim: Neighbouring cells in images often overlap.
source: A particular difficulty is identifying cell boundaries because neighbouring cells in images often overlap: like other microbes, yeast grows in colonies.
evidence: Statement based on observation of yeast growth behavior

claim: Substantial and frequent overlaps between buds and neighbouring cells occur in ALCATRAS microfluidic devices.
source: We observe substantial and frequent overlaps between buds and neighbouring cells in ALCATRAS microfluidic devices (Crane et al., 2014).
evidence: Direct observation by the authors

claim: Overlap is a widespread problem in yeast microscopy images.
source: Inspecting images obtained by others, we believe overlap is a widespread, if undeclared, problem: it occurs during growth in the commercial CellASIC devices (Wood and Doncic, 2019; Dietler et al., 2020), against an agar substrate (Falconnet et al., 2011; Soifer et al., 2016), in a microfluidic dissection platform (Litsios et al., 2019), and in microfluidic devices requiring cells to be attached to the cover slip (Hansen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies showing overlap in different experimental setups

claim: Only a few algorithms allow for overlaps in yeast cell segmentation.
source: Yet only a few algorithms allow for overlaps (Bakker et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bakker et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2019

claim: Software to automatically identify and track cells in bright-field and phase-contrast images is well established.
source: despite software to automatically identify and track cells in bright-field and phase-contrast images being well established (Gordon et al., 2007; Falconnet et al., 2011; Versari et al., 2017; Bakker et al., 2018; Wood and Doncic, 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple established methods

claim: Deep learning has enhanced cell identification and tracking software.
source: and enhanced with deep learning (Falk et al., 2019; Lu et al., 2019; Dietler et al., 2020; Stringer et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent deep learning methods

claim: U-net identifies which pixels in an image are likely from cells.
source: For example, the convolutional neural network U-net (Ronneberger et al., 2015a), a workhorse in biomedical image processing, identifies which pixels in an image are likely from cells
evidence: Supported by citation to Ronneberger et al., 2015a and description of U-net functionality

claim: Assigning lineages and births is often performed manually or through fluorescent markers.
source: Furthermore, assigning lineages and births is often performed manually (Ferrezuelo et al., 2012; Chandler-Brown et al., 2017) or through fluorescent markers (Soifer et al., 2016; Garmendia-Torres et al., 2018; Cuny et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies using these approaches

claim: BABY is a complete pipeline to determine single-cell growth rates from label-free images of budding yeast.
source: Here, we describe the Birth Annotator for Budding Yeast (BABY), a complete pipeline to determine single-cell growth rates from label-free images of budding yeast.
evidence: Direct statement of the algorithm's purpose and capabilities

claim: BABY resolves instances of overlapping cells by extending the U-net architecture with custom training targets.
source: BABY resolves instances of overlapping cells – buds, particularly small ones, usually overlap with their mothers or neighbours – by extending the U-net architecture with custom training targets and then applying additional image processing.
evidence: Description of BABY's technical approach

claim: BABY tracks cells between time points with a machine-learning algorithm.
source: It tracks cells between time points with a machine-learning algorithm, which is able to resolve any large movements of cells from one image to the next
evidence: Description of BABY's tracking capability

claim: BABY assigns buds to their mothers by identifying bud necks.
source: and assigns buds to their mothers, informed by the U-net. These innovations improve performance.
evidence: Description of BABY's lineage assignment capability

claim: BABY produces high-fidelity time series of the volumes of both mother cells and buds.
source: BABY produces high-fidelity time series of the volumes of both mother cells and buds and so the instantaneous growth rates of single cells.
evidence: Statement of BABY's output capabilities

claim: There is a peak in growth rate during the S/G2/M phase of the cell cycle.
source: Using BABY, we see a peak in growth rate during the S/G2/M phase of the cell cycle
evidence: Observation made using BABY algorithm

claim: The peak in growth rate indicates where the bud's growth transitions from being sizer- to timer-controlled.
source: and show that this peak indicates where the bud's growth transitions from being sizer- to timer-controlled.
evidence: Interpretation of data obtained using BABY

claim: Fluctuations in Sfp1's nuclear concentration correlate with but precede those in growth rate.
source: Studying Sfp1, an activator of ribosome synthesis, we observe that fluctuations in this regulator's nuclear concentration correlate with but precede those in growth rate.
evidence: Observation from experiments using BABY

claim: BABY enables real-time control of experiments based on growth rate.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that BABY enables real-time control, running an experiment where changes in the extracellular medium are triggered automatically when the growth of the imaged cells crosses a pre-determined threshold.
evidence: Demonstration experiment performed by the authors

claim: Segmenting asymmetrically dividing cells, such as budding yeast, is challenging.
source: Segmenting asymmetrically dividing cells, such as budding yeast, is challenging.
evidence: Statement of the computational challenge

claim: The differing sizes of the mothers and buds makes each appear and behave distinctly.
source: The differing sizes of the mothers and buds makes each appear and behave distinctly, yet identifying buds is crucial because they have the fastest growth rates (Ferrezuelo et al., 2012; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citation and reference to figure showing growth rate data

claim: Buds imaged in a single Z section often appear to overlap with their mother and neighbouring cells when constrained in a microfluidic device.
source: Even when constrained in a microfluidic device, buds imaged in a single Z section often appear to overlap with their mother and neighbouring cells (Figure 1a and b).
evidence: Observation supported by reference to Figure 1a and b

claim: Buds move more in the Z-axis relative to mother cells, changing how they appear in bright-field images.
source: Buds also move more in the Z-axis relative to mother cells, changing how they appear in bright-field images (Figure 1c).
evidence: Observation supported by reference to Figure 1c

claim: BABY uses a U-net, a convolutional neural network.
source: Like others, we use a U-net, a convolutional neural network (CNN) with an architecture that aims to balance accuracy with simplicity (Ronneberger et al., 2015a)
evidence: Description of the technical approach with citation

claim: BABY's main innovation is in the choice of training targets.
source: and our main innovation is in the choice of training targets.
evidence: Statement of the key innovation

claim: BABY can predict overlapping outlines from a single 2D image.
source: although BABY can predict overlapping outlines from a single 2D image, and we train on single images.
evidence: Statement of BABY's capability

claim: How much and how often cells overlap depends on their size.
source: Inspecting cells, we noted that how much and how often they overlap depends on their size (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: Observation by the authors, supported by reference to Appendix figure

claim: Most overlaps occur between mid-sized cells and buds with sizes in the range expected for fast growth.
source: Most overlaps occur between mid-sized cells and buds with sizes in the range expected for fast growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Observation supported by reference to figure

claim: BABY divides training data into three categories based on cell size.
source: We therefore divided our training data into three categories based on cell size.
evidence: Description of the training data preparation method

claim: BABY applies morphological erosion to decrease overlaps in training images.
source: We decreased any remaining overlaps in these training images by applying a morphological erosion (Figure 2b; Appendix 1—figures 1 and 2), shrinking the cells by removing pixels from their boundaries.
evidence: Description of image processing technique with figure references

claim: The bud neck helps to identify which bud belongs to which cell.
source: A final target is the 'bud neck' (Figure 2e), which helps to identify which bud belongs to which cell.
evidence: Description of a training target with figure reference

claim: Cytokinesis is sometimes visible as a darkening of the bud neck in bright-field images.
source: In bright-field images, cytokinesis is sometimes visible as a darkening of the bud neck, indicating that these images contain information on cytokinesis that the U-net can potentially learn.
evidence: Observation about bright-field imaging

claim: BABY achieved high accuracy for predicting the cell interiors early in training and with around 600 training images.
source: Using a four-layer U-net, we achieved high accuracy for predicting the cell interiors early in training and with around 600 training images (1,813 annotated cells in total; Figure 2c & Appendix 1—figure 3c).
evidence: Performance results with figure references

claim: BABY parameterises cell boundaries using a radial representation.
source: Second, and like the StarDist (Schmidt et al., 2018) and DISCO algorithms (Bakker et al., 2018), we parameterise the cell boundaries using a radial representation because we expect yeast cells to appear elliptical – although we can describe any star-convex shape.
evidence: Description of the boundary representation method with citations

claim: BABY outperforms alternatives in cell segmentation.
source: We find that BABY outperforms alternatives (Figure 3a), even when we retrain these alternatives with the BABY training data.
evidence: Comparison results with figure reference

claim: For larger cell sizes, BABY performs comparably with Cellpose and YeaZ.
source: For larger cell sizes, BABY performs comparably with two algorithms based on deep learning: Cellpose (Stringer et al., 2021; Pachitariu and Stringer, 2022), a generalist algorithm, and YeaZ (Dietler et al., 2020), an algorithm optimised for yeast.
evidence: Comparison results with citations

claim: For smaller cell sizes, BABY performs better than Cellpose and YeaZ, identifying buds overlapping with mother cells that both miss.
source: For smaller cell sizes, BABY performs better, identifying buds overlapping with mother cells that both Cellpose and YeaZ miss (Figure 3b).
evidence: Comparison results with figure reference

claim: BABY performs competitively on time-lapse images of yeast microcolonies.
source: To assess its generality, we turned to time-lapse images of yeast microcolonies, training a BABY model on only 6% of the annotated microcolony training data provided by YeaZ and evaluating its performance on the remaining images. BABY performs competitively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Generalization test results with figure reference

claim: BABY finds a higher fraction of complete tracks than either YeaZ or Cellpose combined with btrack.
source: BABY finds a higher fraction of complete tracks than either YeaZ or Cellpose, an algorithm only for segmentation and trained on BABY data, combined with btrack (Ulicna et al., 2021), a tracking algorithm.
evidence: Tracking performance comparison with citation

claim: BABY estimates growth rates more reliably than other algorithms.
source: BABY estimates growth rates more reliably than other algorithms (Figure 3e).
evidence: Growth rate estimation comparison with figure reference

claim: BABY best reproduces the growth rates derived from manually curated ground truth.
source: BABY best reproduces the growth rates derived from this ground truth.
evidence: Validation against ground truth data

claim: Cellular growth has two phases: during G1, the mother's growth rate peaks; during S/G2/M, the bud dominates growth with its growth rate peaking approximately midway to cytokinesis.
source: Using a fluorescent marker for cytokinesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 6a), we observed that cellular growth has two phases (Figure 3—figure supplement 6b–c). During G1, the mother's growth rate peaks; during S/G2/M, which we identify by the cells having buds, the bud dominates growth with its growth rate peaking approximately midway to cytokinesis (Ferrezuelo et al., 2012).
evidence: Observation from experiments with figure references and citation

claim: The maximal growth rate of buds occurs at similar times relative to cytokinesis despite substantial differences in the duration of the S/G2/M phases in different carbon sources.
source: Comparing growth rates over S/G2/M for buds in different carbon sources, we found that the maximal growth rate occurs at similar times relative to cytokinesis despite substantial differences in the duration of the S/G2/M phases (Figure 4a).
evidence: Experimental observation with figure reference

claim: Daughters born in rich media are larger than those born in poor media.
source: Daughters born in rich media are larger than those born in poor media, and some of this regulation occurs during S/G2/M (Johnston et al., 1977; Jorgensen et al., 2004; Leitao and Kellogg, 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by citations

claim: Buds have similar sizes when their growth rates peak in all carbon sources.
source: Compared to how their sizes vary immediately after cytokinesis, buds have similar sizes when their growth rates peak — in all carbon sources (Figure 4b)
evidence: Experimental observation with figure reference

claim: The bud's average growth rate correlates positively with the volume of the daughter it becomes.
source: During the subsequent constant time to cytokinesis, the faster growth in richer carbon sources would then generate larger daughters, and we observe that the bud's average growth rate correlates positively with the volume of the daughter it becomes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental observation with figure reference

claim: Cells likely implement some size regulation in S/G2/M as they approach cytokinesis.
source: Cells likely therefore implement some size regulation in S/G2/M as they approach cytokinesis.
evidence: Inference from experimental data

claim: Bud growth is likely first sizer- then timer-controlled.
source: our data suggest a sequential mechanism to match size to growth rate, with a nutrient-independent sizer followed by a nutrient-dependent timer.
evidence: Inference from experimental data

claim: Sfp1 promotes the synthesis of ribosomes by activating the ribosomal protein (RP) and ribosome biogenesis (RiBi) genes.
source: Sfp1 promotes the synthesis of ribosomes by activating the ribosomal protein (RP) and ribosome biogenesis (RiBi) genes (Jorgensen et al., 2004; Albert et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: Sfp1 enters the nucleus upon being phosphorylated directly by TORC1 and likely protein kinase A.
source: Upon being phosphorylated directly by TORC1 and likely protein kinase A (Jorgensen et al., 2004; Lempiäinen et al., 2009; Singh and Tyers, 2009) – two conserved nutrient-sensing kinases, Sfp1 enters the nucleus (Figure 5a).
evidence: Supported by citations and figure reference

claim: In steady-state conditions, levels of ribosomes positively correlate with growth rate.
source: In steady-state conditions, levels of ribosomes positively correlate with growth rate (Metzl-Raz et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Sfp1 responds quickly to both up- and downshifts in nutrients.
source: Shifting cells from glucose to the poorer carbon source palatinose and back again, we observed that Sfp1 responds quickly to both the up- and downshifts
evidence: Experimental observation

claim: Growth rate responds as quickly to downshifts as Sfp1, but more slowly to upshifts.
source: and that growth rate responds as quickly to downshifts, but more slowly to upshifts (Figure 5b).
evidence: Experimental observation with figure reference

claim: Downshift half-times are less variable than those for upshifts, consistent with fast post-translational regulation.
source: and downshift half-times are less variable than those for upshifts, consistent with fast post-translational regulation.
evidence: Observation and interpretation from experimental data

claim: Fluctuations in Sfp1 lead those in growth rate by an average of 25 min in glucose and by 50 min in palatinose.
source: Cross-correlating nuclear Sfp1 with growth rate shows that fluctuations in Sfp1 do lead those in growth rate, by an average of 25 min in glucose and by 50 min in palatinose (Figure 5d).
evidence: Quantitative analysis from experimental data with figure reference

claim: The weak strength of correlation between Sfp1 and growth rate suggests substantial control besides Sfp1.
source: Nevertheless, the weak strength of this correlation suggests substantial control besides Sfp1.
evidence: Inference from correlation analysis

claim: During the downshift, the growth rate transiently drops to zero irrespective of a cell's stage in the cell cycle.
source: During the downshift, we note that the growth rate transiently drops to zero (Figure 5b), irrespective of a cell's stage in the cell cycle (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Experimental observation with figure references

claim: There is a coincident rise in the fraction of cells in G1 during the downshift, suggesting that cells arrest in that phase.
source: and there is a coincident rise in the fraction of cells in G1 (Figure 5b bottom), suggesting that cells arrest in that phase.
evidence: Experimental observation with figure reference and interpretation

claim: BABY's speed and accuracy enables cells to be identified in images and their growth rates estimated during an experiment.
source: With BABY, we can use growth rate as a control variable in real time because BABY's speed and accuracy enables cells to be identified in images and their growth rates estimated during an experiment (Figure 6a).
evidence: Demonstration of BABY's capability with figure reference

claim: BABY can automatically determine the fraction of cells that have escaped the lag at each time point.
source: Using BABY, we automatically determined the fraction of cells that have escaped the lag at each time point — those cells that have at least one bud or daughter whose growth rate exceeds a threshold (Figure 6b).
evidence: Demonstration experiment with figure reference

claim: All cells resume dividing in glucose and initially grow synchronously because of the rapid change of media.
source: We note that all cells resume dividing in glucose and initially grow synchronously because of the rapid change of media.
evidence: Observation from real-time control experiment

claim: BABY allows single-cell fluorescence and growth rates to be control variables.
source: Unlike previous approaches though, which typically measure fluorescence, BABY not only allows single-cell fluorescence but also growth rates to be control variables
evidence: Statement of BABY's capability compared to previous approaches

claim: Training data for the segmentation and bud assignment models comprises bright-field time-lapse images of yeast cells and manually curated annotations.
source: Training data for the segmentation and bud assignment models comprises bright-field time-lapse images of yeast cells and manually curated annotations: a bit-mask outline for each cell (a binary image with the pixels constituting the cell marked with ones) and its associated tracking label and lineage assignment, if any.
evidence: Description of training data

claim: The training data includes a total of 3233 annotated cell outlines distributed across 1028 time points, 130 traps, and 28 fields-of-view.
source: These images were from six independent experiments and annotated by three different people and include a total of 3233 annotated cell outlines distributed across 1028 time points, 130 traps, and 28 fields-of-view.
evidence: Quantitative description of training data

claim: All strains used in the curated training images were derivatives of BY4741.
source: Strains included in the curated training images were all derivatives of BY4741 (Brachmann et al., 1998).
evidence: Description of strains with citation
